extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and professional copy editors, authors, publishers, and students learning about editorial practice
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and standards for copy editing manuscripts and online copy to improve readability, correctness, consistency, and conformity to house style across print and digital media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copy editing levels (light, medium, heavy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Copy editing has three levels: light, medium, and heavy. Depending on the budget and scheduling of the publication, the publisher will let the copy editor know what level of editing to employ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chosen type of editing helps the copy editor prioritize efforts; light edits are minimal mechanical fixes, medium includes sentence-level smoothing, heavy may include substantial remedial work on style and clarity. Level selection is driven by publisher instructions, budget, and schedule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical editing
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanical editing is the process of closely reading a piece of writing for consistency, either internally or in accordance with the publisher's house style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanical editors work with abbreviations and acronyms; additional elements such as charts, tables, and graphs; capitalization; footnotes and endnotes; hyphenation; italicization (appropriate use of emphasis and choice of typeface category); numbers and numerals; punctuation; quotations; and spelling. Also includes page numbers, headers and footers, initialisms, underscoring, and other formatting elements. Use a recognized style guide (New Oxford, Chicago Manual, Canadian Style) or an in-house style; where conventions are subjective, exercise editorial judgement or follow publisher preference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial style conformity
rubrics_metrics.description: The heart of copyediting consists of making a manuscript conform to an editorial style (house style).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial style includes spelling, hyphenation, capitalization, punctuation, treatment of numbers and numerals, treatment of quotations, use of abbreviations and acronyms, use of italics and bold type, treatment of special elements (headings, lists, tables, charts, and graphs), and format of footnotes/endnotes and other documentation. Ensure consistent application throughout the manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grammar and usage — enforce rules while respecting author preference
rubrics_metrics.description: The goal of the copy editor is to enforce inviolable rules while respecting personal stylistic preferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because language conventions vary and prescriptive sources disagree, copy editors are encouraged to respect the author's preference when acceptable. Balance enforcement of grammatical rules with sensitivity to the author's voice; avoid treating corrections as a challenge to the writer's identity. Apply house style when required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content editing (reorganizing and restructuring)
rubrics_metrics.description: Content editing consists of reorganizing or restructuring a document and fixing inconsistent parts of the content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content editors may rewrite or heavily edit to fix issues; copy editors should point out especially difficult passages to the author for resolution. Copy editors are not generally responsible for full substantive/developmental editing but may highlight structural problems and query the author. When knowledgeable about the subject, limited fact-checking (e.g., obvious date or year discrepancies) is acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-checking and legal/bias checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Although not responsible for factual correctness, copy editors can provide comments on known untrue information and must point out biased language and material that might form the basis for libel, invasion of privacy, or obscenity claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copy editors may perform fact-checking when they know the subject matter. For biased language, distinguish between intentionally-held politically incorrect views and marginalizing/offensive language; permit intentional controversial views but censor or flag language that is marginalizing or could cause legal exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlating parts and cross-checking
rubrics_metrics.description: Copy editors must correlate the parts within manuscripts by verifying cross-references and checking numbering and placement of elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tasks include: verify cross-references; check numbering of footnotes/endnotes, tables and illustrations; specify placement of tables and illustrations; check content of illustrations against captions and text; read list of illustrations against actual figures and captions; read the table of contents against the manuscript; check footnotes/endnotes and in-text citations against the bibliography; and check alphabetization of bibliography/reference list. Special cross-checking may be required for how-to texts (equipment lists vs instructions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Typecoding and identification of elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Typecoding is the process of identifying which sections of the manuscript are not regular running text (elements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify elements such as part and chapter numbers, titles and subtitles, headings and subheadings, lists, extracts, displayed equations, table numbers, source lines, footnotes, figure numbers and captions. Mark type codes for the publication designer (penciled in margins for hard-copy; inserted tags or markers for on-screen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissions and copyright checks
rubrics_metrics.description: If the manuscript contains long quotations or reprinted material that is under copyright, the copy editor should remind the author to acquire permission to reprint those quotations and other previously published material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This applies to tables, charts, graphs, illustrations and unpublished materials (letters, diaries) where rules vary; flag potential copyright issues early so permissions can be obtained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial processes: marking, querying, record-keeping, cleanup
rubrics_metrics.description: Basic procedures every copy editor must follow: marking changes, querying the author/editorial coordinator, keeping track of editorial decisions, and incorporating the author's review into a final document (cleanup).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop consistent systems for these tasks; adapt traditional procedures to both hard-copy and on-screen workflows. Record decisions in a manner accessible to the production team and ensure final cleanup incorporates author responses and tracked changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard-copy editing conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional markup copy editing (hard-copy) involves writing corrections directly in the text and leaving margins for queries, using bright ink so changes are clearly visible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All parties (editor, author, typesetter, proofreader) must understand the markup symbols. Hard-copy skill remains important for employment tests and when electronic exchange isn't possible. Use the margin for queries and preserve manuscript integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: On-screen editing practices
rubrics_metrics.description: On-screen editing differs from hard-copy editing: copy the author's files and preserve originals; use word-processor markup tools; edit cleanly and maintain proper line spacing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use track changes or equivalent; avoid saving partial words; be careful with line and page breaks; be familiar with how word processors display markups. On-screen workflows allow searching, spellcheckers, and generating clean copies, but require different habits than pencil marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Querying: when and how to ask authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Copy editors often need to query authors to address questions, comments, or explanations; queries can be placed in margins or comments when on screen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider timing, length, and tone of queries—querying too often or too seldom, cryptically, or sarcastically can harm the editor–author relationship. Keep queries clear, polite, and purposeful; prioritize queries that affect meaning, legal risk, or factual accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goals and stakeholders — the 'cardinal C' and the 4 Cs
rubrics_metrics.description: A copy editor serves three constituencies—the author, the publisher, and the readers—with the shared goal of producing an error-free publication and improving the reader experience by reducing extraneous cognitive load.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive to improve clarity, coherence, consistency and correctness (the '4 Cs'), which serve the copy editor's 'cardinal C' of communication. Balance the often-competing needs of authorial voice, publisher requirements, and reader comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing copy editing from other editing types
rubrics_metrics.description: Copy editing focuses on clarity, accuracy, consistency and readability and conformity with house style; it is distinct from substantive (developmental), line editing, and proofreading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantive editing addresses structure, pacing, and content organization and may reorder sections or suggest new content. Line editing is more in-depth on sentence- and paragraph-level craft to enhance prose and voice. Proofreading is the final check for typographical, grammatical and formatting errors. Know the boundaries and when to escalate to developmental editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemporary digital competencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern copy editors are often required to edit for digital as well as print versions and must understand multimedia and web technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Digital copy editing may require knowledge of SEO, HTML, CSS, RSS feeds, social media, and creative tools (Adobe InDesign, Illustrator, QuarkXPress, Affinity Publisher, Photoshop). Copy editors may also need to consider multimedia elements (video, images, audio) and accessibility needs (alt text, transcripts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritization, speed, and back-editing risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Copy editing can slow publication; in fast digital workflows publishers sometimes publish first and edit later ('back-editing').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and publishers must prioritize which pieces get pre-publication edits based on factors like traffic and importance. Be aware that lack of prepublication copyediting can affect quality and credibility; plan for triage and post-publication cleanup where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traits, skills and training for copy editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Copy editors often have degrees in journalism, communications, or the language they edit and may seek additional topical knowledge (e.g., statistics). Training programs, internships, and professional organizations offer mid-career training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hiring/tests often assess grammar, punctuation, style (AP, house style), headline writing, infographic editing, journalism ethics, and software skills. Continuous learning in digital tools and domain knowledge (statistics, subject-matter familiarity) improves accuracy and employability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and ethical boundaries (no ghostwriting/developmental editing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Copy editors are not licensed to rewrite a text line by line or to prepare material on an author's behalf (ghostwriting) and do not normally engage in developmental editing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copy editors should query structural/organizational problems but not unilaterally fix them; avoid creating original content for another person's byline. If developmental work is required, recommend or coordinate with appropriate editorial services.
